html:
The equal-field system was a way of sharing out farmland used in China from 485 to the mid 700s. The state owned the land and gave each farming household fields according to the number of its adults, in return for taxes and labour.

It was introduced by Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei (Toba Wei), under the guidance of the Empress Dowager Feng. After decades of war, much land in the north lay empty, while great families held many dependants. The system put people back on the land and onto the tax rolls.

Each adult man received fields for grain, which went back to the state at his death or old age, plus fields for mulberry trees or hemp that could be passed on. The Sui and Tang kept the system, and Japan copied it in the Taika Reform.

It broke down as the population grew and land ran short, and great estates grew again. After the An Lushan Rebellion wrecked the registers, the Tang replaced it in 780 with the two-tax system, based on land and property.
sum: The equal-field system was a way of sharing out farmland used in China from 485 to the mid 700s. The state owned the land and gave each farming household fields according to the number of its adults, in return for taxes and labour.
